headline: This law lets federal officials reopen burial decisions at VA and Arlington cemeteries for people who may have committed capital crimes but were never convicted, and it directs removal of one specific veteran's remains.
what_it_does: The law allows the VA Secretary or the Army Secretary to reconsider an interment or memorial decision if they learn a person may have committed a federal or state capital crime but was never convicted because the person died or fled before trial. After a hearing, if the official finds the person committed the crime, the official must notify the family or other person who arranged the burial, who then has 60 days to file a disagreement that starts appeal review. Once the decision is final, the official may remove the remains or memorial marker. The law also requires written notice of a conviction before a person convicted of a capital crime can be buried or memorialized, instead of before an application is approved. Finally, it directs the VA Secretary to disinter Michael LaShawn Anderson from Fort Custer National Cemetery in Michigan, notify his next of kin, and release the remains to them or arrange other disposition.

who_it_affects.group: Next of kin of people buried or memorialized in VA national cemeteries or Arlington National Cemetery
who_it_affects.how: They can receive notice of a proposed removal of remains or a memorial marker and have 60 days to file a disagreement that triggers appeal review.
They must be notified of the planned disinterment of his remains from Fort Custer National Cemetery and may receive the remains or have them handled by the VA.

who_it_affects.group: Veterans and families applying for burial in national cemeteries
who_it_affects.how: Burial or memorialization of a person convicted of a capital crime requires written notice of the conviction before it takes place.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted December 20, 2013, with the provisions effective on that date.
